sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

# Surfing Pelican

An animated, non-interactive Three.js scene of a pelican riding a surfboard
across an endless, procedurally generated ocean.

Open `index.html` and watch. There are no controls, no network requests and no
stored state — everything is generated in code at runtime.

## What's in the scene

- **Ocean** — a GPU-displaced plane. The vertex shader sums several travelling
  sine waves to build the swell, derives the surface normal from finite
  differences, and the fragment shader adds fresnel sky reflection, a sun
  glint, translucent crests and foam. The plane is panned in the shader so the
  water never runs out.
- **Pelican** — modelled entirely from primitives (sphere, cone, tube,
  extruded wing and board shapes). It samples the exact same wave function as
  the water, so it sits on the surface, tilts with the local slope, rolls as it
  carves, and its head, body and wings idle with small procedural motions.
- **Spray** — a GPU point system that throws droplets off the tail of the board.
- **Sky & life** — a painted equirectangular sky is used for the background and,
  via `PMREMGenerator`, for image-based lighting. Billboard clouds drift past
  and a handful of distant gulls circle overhead.

## Files

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `index.html` | Page shell, canvas and inline styles. |
| `main.js` | Renderer, camera, animation loop and scene assembly. |
| `waves.js` | Shared wave math (JS) and its GLSL twin. |
| `ocean.js` | Procedural water mesh and shaders. |
| `pelican.js` | The bird, surfboard and materials. |
| `spray.js` | Particle spray. |
| `environment.js` | Sky, lighting, clouds and birds. |

## Running

The source uses bare ESM imports, so serve the folder over HTTP (module
scripts do not load from `file://`):

```sh
npx serve .
# or
python3 -m http.server
```

The page is designed to be bundled into a single self-contained HTML file with
esbuild. The bundle entry is `main.js`:

```sh
esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=dist/main.js
```

## Surfing Pelican 🏄

An animated, non-interactive Three.js ocean scene with a procedurally-modelled pelican riding a surfboard. No controls, no network, no storage — all geometry, textures, and animation are generated in code.

### Files created
- **`index.html`** — canvas + inline CSS + `<script type="module" src="main.js">`
- **`main.js`** — renderer, camera, animation loop, scene assembly
- **`waves.js`** — shared wave math in JS with a matching GLSL twin
- **`ocean.js`** — GPU-displaced water (custom vertex/fragment shaders)
- **`pelican.js`** — bird, surfboard, and materials from primitives
- **`spray.js`** — particle spray
- **`environment.js`** — painted sky, IBL lighting, clouds, distant gulls
- **`README.md`**, `package.json` (depends on `three`)

### How it works
- **Water**: a plane whose vertices are displaced by a sum of travelling sine waves in the vertex shader. Normals come from finite differences of the same function; the fragment shader adds fresnel sky reflection, a tight sun glint, translucent crests, and broken-up foam. The plane is panned in-shader from a snapped camera position, so the ocean is endless.
- **Rider**: the pelican samples *the exact same wave function on the CPU* (kept in sync by generating the GLSL from the shared constants), so it sits precisely on the surface. It builds an orientation basis from the tangent plane and wave normal, rolls as it carves, and its body, turned head/beak/pouch, and wings have subtle idle motion. Legs and feet stay planted on the board.
- **Extras**: bow spray from a GPU point system, billboard clouds drifting with parallax, circling gulls, and image-based lighting via `PMREMGenerator` from the procedural equirect sky.
